prose.summary: A structural engineer decides how a building or bridge carries load, then proves it on paper before anyone pours concrete. The confusion with civil engineering is fair since both show up on the same job site, but civil handles the roads and drainage around a building while structural handles whether the building itself stands up under wind, snow, and its own weight. The line sharpens once you notice who signs the calculations: that's the license question, and it shapes almost everything else about the career.
prose.day_to_day: Most weeks split into a few days at your desk running models in ETABS and a couple of days in meetings or on calls with architects, contractors, or the rest of the design team. You open the analysis software to check a beam size or a connection, then switch to Revit to make sure the framing matches what the architect drew (it often doesn't, on the first pass). There's a construction administration piece too: reviewing shop drawings, answering an RFI from a contractor who found a conflict in the field, occasionally driving out to look at something that doesn't match the plans. The moment people wait for is when a permit set finally gets stamped, or when a contractor calls to say the steel went up clean and nothing needed a field fix. Training junior engineers eats a real chunk of time once you're a few years in, since someone has to teach the next person how to read a moment diagram without flinching. The rest is documentation: calc packages, details, revisions, the paper trail that makes the design defensible five years later if someone asks why a beam is the size it is.
prose.work_environment: The default setting is an office, at a desk, with two or three monitors running analysis software and drawings side by side. Site visits happen but they're occasional, not constant, which is part of why remote work has room here (32 percent of postings allow it) even though the job still touches physical buildings. Deadlines cluster around permit submissions and bid dates, and the bad weeks are the ones where a client moves a deadline up or a plan check comes back with corrections the night before a submission. Overtime shows up in bursts tied to project milestones rather than as a constant, and the work is desk-bound enough that a laptop and a VPN into the firm's server covers most of it, with the office reserved for the meetings that need a whiteboard.
prose.getting_in: The degree comes first: an ABET-accredited engineering degree, which the postings treat as close to universal even though a handful list it as preferred rather than required. After that you sit the FE exam, then spend around four years working under a licensed engineer before you're eligible for the PE exam in your discipline. That experience clock, not the exams themselves, is what sets the floor: most people could pass the PE sooner than they're allowed to sit for it. The whole path runs 4 to 6 years from graduation, and the median engineer in these postings already has 5 years in, which tells you how much of this field is post-license hiring. The common stall point is the years between FE and PE, where the work is real engineering but the title and pay lag behind it; firms that offer certification support (a minority, but they exist) are worth weighting for that reason alone.
prose.ladder: Early on you own pieces: a beam line, a connection detail, a section of the calc package someone else is assembling. The first real step up is being handed a project to run start to finish, coordinating with the architect and other engineers instead of just producing your piece of the model, and that usually tracks with getting your PE. After that the ladder forks: one path stays technical, running increasingly complex analysis and becoming the person junior engineers ask when something doesn't converge, the other moves into project management and eventually business development, chasing the next job instead of just doing the current one. Both paths exist inside the same firm, and around 10 years in is when most people know which one they're on.
prose.suits: People who like this work tend to like the moment a model finally clashes clean, or the satisfaction of a detail that solves three problems at once (loads, cost, and something the architect wanted aesthetically). It rewards people who can hold a lot of numbers in their head while also caring about how a stair looks, because both things end up on the same drawing. The ones who leave are usually looking for faster feedback than construction gives: a building takes years from sketch to occupancy, and if you want to see the result of your work in weeks rather than years, this isn't it. People who wanted to design rather than verify sometimes drift toward architecture instead, since structural work is more about proving something is safe than about originating its shape.
prose.misconceptions: People assume structural engineers design the building's appearance, when mostly they're making sure the shape someone else drew doesn't fall down, which is a very different skill and a much narrower brief. Another one: that it's a desk job free of liability concerns once you're not the one signing drawings. Even without a PE, your calculations feed into someone else's stamp, and firms track that chain closely because it's their license on the line too.
prose.who_qualifies: Architects show the strongest overlap (43 percent match), since both read the same drawings and think in terms of spans, loads, and code compliance, though architects moving over need to build actual analysis skills rather than just spatial judgment. MEP engineers and civil engineers also convert well, carrying over building codes knowledge and construction administration experience, while BIM managers bring the Revit and coordination fluency that's increasingly load-bearing for the job itself. What doesn't transfer automatically from any of these is the calculation discipline: knowing where a formula applies and where it quietly doesn't.
prose.what_the_numbers_miss: None of this shows what it feels like to be the engineer of record on a building that's already occupied, the particular weight of knowing your stamp is on a document that outlives your involvement with the project. It also can't measure how much of the job is persuasion: convincing an architect that a column has to go where you say it goes, not where they drew it.

steps.how: This is a 4-year undergraduate degree in civil or structural engineering; ABET accreditation matters because most state boards require it for licensure later. You're done when you have the degree in hand, though some people add a structural-focused master's if they want deeper analysis coursework before entering the workforce.

steps.do: Pass the FE exam before or at graduation
steps.how: The Fundamentals of Engineering exam is typically taken in the final year of the degree or right after; it's a single computer-based test covering general engineering topics. Passing it makes you an EIT (Engineer in Training) and starts the clock toward PE eligibility.

steps.do: Work under a licensed PE for ~4 years
steps.how: This is the long step: roughly four years of documented experience under a licensed structural or civil engineer, doing real design work that they review and sign. You're done when your supervising PE can verify the hours and the experience covers a range of structural systems, not just one repeated task.

steps.do: Sit and pass the PE exam in structural
steps.how: This is a discipline-specific exam administered through NCEES and state boards, usually taken once the experience requirement is met. Passing it is what lets you sign and seal drawings yourself, which is the gate that separates a staff engineer from an engineer of record.

steps.do: Build fluency in ETABS and Revit specifically
steps.how: These two show up in 42 and 61 percent of postings respectively, so a portfolio piece that shows a full workflow (model in ETABS, coordinated framing in Revit, resolved clashes) does more for hiring than a list of software names on a resume. This runs alongside the degree and early work experience rather than after it.

prose.tools: Revit and ETABS are the two real gatekeepers, showing up in 61 and 42 percent of postings, and a firm will assume you can pick up their specific modeling standards fast if you already know both. Structural analysis knowledge and building codes fluency matter as much as any software, since the tools are only as good as the engineer telling them what to check. FEA (finite element analysis) shows up in about a quarter of postings and tends to gate the more specialized, complex-geometry work. The direction of travel is toward tighter BIM coordination, meaning the Revit model isn't just a drawing anymore, it's the shared source of truth across architect, structural, and MEP teams.

industries.name: Structural engineering consulting firms
industries.note: The most common employer; project-based work across many building types, with exposure to a wide range of structural systems early in a career.

industries.name: General architecture/engineering (A/E) firms
industries.note: Structural sits inside a larger firm alongside architects and MEP engineers, meaning tighter day-to-day coordination and less standalone structural specialization.

industries.name: Construction and general contracting companies
industries.note: In-house structural engineers here focus more on construction administration and field problem-solving than on original design work.

industries.name: Government and infrastructure agencies
industries.note: Slower-paced, code-review or public-works-heavy work, often with more job security and less overtime than consulting.

specializations.name: Seismic retrofit and analysis
specializations.why: Regions with older building stock and updated seismic codes need engineers who specialize in retrofitting existing structures, a technically distinct skill from new-building design that pays a premium in the right markets.

specializations.name: Tall building and high-rise structural design
specializations.why: Requires deep FEA and wind-load expertise beyond standard building code checks; a small number of firms concentrate this work and hire specifically for it.

specializations.name: BIM/VDC coordination for structural teams
specializations.why: As Revit fluency becomes table stakes, the engineers who can manage the model as a coordination tool across disciplines (not just draft in it) are increasingly hired into BIM manager-adjacent roles.

pros: There's a specific, visible payoff to the work: you can drive past a building years later and know exactly why that column is where it is.
The path from EIT to PE is clearly marked, so you always know how far along you are rather than guessing at an informal ladder.
Generous PTO shows up in 65 percent of postings, which is unusually high and reflects a field that doesn't run on always-on urgency outside of deadline weeks.
The work rewards getting better at it in a way that's easy to notice: models converge faster, details need fewer revisions, contractors call less often with problems you already anticipated.
cons: The gap between finishing your degree and getting licensed runs years, and the pay and title often lag behind the responsibility you're already carrying.
Liability sits with the profession in a way that's hard to shake off after hours; a mistake in a calc package doesn't stay at the office.
Deadline weeks around permit submissions can be genuinely brutal, with corrections landing the night before a deadline more often than anyone would like.
Coordination with architects means regularly explaining, again, why their vision needs a column they didn't want, which wears on people who dislike repeated negotiation.

faq.q: how long does it take to become a licensed structural engineer
faq.a: Typically 4 to 6 years from graduation, and the experience requirement (about 4 years under a licensed engineer), not the exams, is what sets that floor. Most people could pass the PE exam earlier than they're eligible to sit for it.

faq.q: can you be a structural engineer without a PE license
faq.a: Yes, for a lot of the actual work: product and coordination roles hire unlicensed engineers regularly, since the PE only gates who can sign and seal drawings, not who can do the analysis. You'll eventually hit a ceiling without it if you want to run projects as engineer of record.

faq.q: structural engineer vs civil engineer, what's the difference
faq.a: Structural engineers focus on whether a building or bridge itself can carry its loads; civil engineers handle the broader site, roads, drainage, and infrastructure around it. Civil Engineer is also the most common move out of structural, sharing a 45 percent skill match, but it requires its own license path.

Some of it, yes: about 32 percent of postings allow remote work, since a lot of the job is modeling and drawing review that doesn't require physical presence. Site visits and in-person coordination meetings still pull people back to an office or a job site periodically.

faq.q: what does a structural engineer get paid starting out vs later
faq.a: The median across measured postings sits at $106k, with the bottom quarter at $87k and the top quarter above $132k, and that spread mostly tracks years of experience and PE status. Early-career pay clusters toward the lower end until licensure, after which it moves up meaningfully.
